spec.title: One claim, three stores, one real engine
spec.intro:
The same eight acme.example users you pulled from the API in module 06 are loaded three ways into
one real SQLite engine: a relational `users` table, a `users_doc` table of JSON documents, and a
`users_kv` key-value table. You are asked to answer ONE control question — "which users lack
MFA?" — in each store, prove you evaluated all eight, then diagnose a SQL-injection break by
running a concatenated query against a parameterized one.

This console is real SQLite running in your browser — the same engine that ships in your phone.
You type SQL; the engine returns real result sets, checked against the engine's own output.
Nothing is invented; the result set is the answer key. The eight users are seeded for you; start
by reading the relational store.
spec.walkthrough_first_input: SELECT email FROM users WHERE mfa_enabled = 0 ORDER BY email;

tasks.instruction:
On the relational store, run a query that returns the `email` of every user who lacks MFA,
ordered by email. The claim "every user has MFA" is a predicate over the `mfa_enabled` column
(0 = off). Read the four users the engine returns.

hints.nudge: A relational predicate filters rows on a column: which column is 0 when MFA is off?

hints.concept: §4.1 — the relational model: a control claim is a predicate over a typed column

hints.reveal: SELECT email FROM users WHERE mfa_enabled = 0 ORDER BY email;

tasks.explain:
Four of the eight users lack MFA. You just evaluated a control claim as a `WHERE` predicate
over a typed column — the relational store's whole strength. The engine returned the rows; no
one screenshotted a dashboard.

tasks.instruction:
Prove completeness: run a query returning the total number of user rows (alias the count `n`),
so you can show you evaluated EVERY account, not a sample. This is the completeness proof the
relational store gives you for free.

hints.nudge: Completeness means 'how many records did I look at in total?' — count them.

hints.concept: §4.3 — completeness in a store: relational COUNT(*) proves the whole set was seen

hints.reveal: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM users;

tasks.explain:
Eight accounts total, four without MFA — and now you can prove the four are out of eight, not
out of an unknown sample. Proving you saw the whole set is half of an audit finding.

tasks.instruction:
Answer the SAME question against the document store `users_doc`, where each user is a JSON
document in the `doc` column. Use `json_extract(doc, '$.field')` to read the email of every
user whose `mfa_enabled` field is 0, ordered by email. Confirm the answer matches t1.

hints.nudge: A document is self-describing — reach a field by its path, not a column name.

hints.concept: §4.2 — the document model: read control-truth by field path with json_extract

hints.reveal: SELECT json_extract(doc, '$.email') AS email FROM users_doc WHERE json_extract(doc, '$.mfa_enabled') = 0 ORDER BY email;

tasks.explain:
The same four users — bob, dave, frank, heidi — fall out of the document store too. The store
changed the REACH (a field path instead of a column), not the TRUTH. That identity is the
lesson: the data model is a choice about access patterns, not about what is true.

tasks.instruction:
Answer it once more against the key-value store `users_kv`, whose value is an opaque blob the
store cannot filter on (e.g. `bob@acme.example|mfa=0|active`). Return the keys `k` whose value
encodes `mfa=0`, ordered by key. Notice you had to know the value's internal format yourself.

hints.nudge: The store can't see inside the value — match the substring the value encodes for MFA-off.

hints.concept: §4.3 — the key-value model: the value is opaque; you enumerate and parse it yourself

hints.reveal: SELECT k FROM users_kv WHERE v LIKE '%|mfa=0|%' ORDER BY k;

tasks.explain:
The same four users by their keys (user:u_002, user:u_004, user:u_006, user:u_008) — but you
matched on the value's internal format because the store is blind to it. Completeness here rests on having scanned
every key, since there is no schema or column to lean on.

tasks.instruction:
Diagnose injection. An email-lookup feature is meant to return ONE user but is built by gluing
input into the query string. Run the CONCATENATED query that results when the input is
`' OR '1'='1` — read how many rows the engine returns versus the one the feature intended.

hints.nudge: The input closes the string early and adds an always-true clause — the store obeys.

hints.concept: §4.5 — SQL injection: concatenating untrusted input makes the store answer a different question

hints.reveal: SELECT email FROM users WHERE email = '' OR '1'='1';

tasks.explain:
The lookup asked for one user and the engine honestly returned all eight — the injected
`OR '1'='1` is always true. The over-broad result set is the SI-10 finding, and it is the
engine's real answer, not your claim.

tasks.instruction:
Now run the PARAMETERIZED form of the same lookup with the same input. Binding the input as a
value means the whole string `' OR '1'='1` is treated as one literal email address — written
out, that is the escaped literal below. Read the empty result set: the control working.

hints.nudge: Bound as a value, the entire input is ONE email string — and no user has that address.

hints.concept: §4.5 — parameterization binds input as a value, so injection becomes a literal that matches nobody

hints.reveal: SELECT email FROM users WHERE email = ''' OR ''1''=''1';

tasks.explain:
Zero rows. Binding the input as a value turned the attack into a harmless literal email address
that matches no user — exactly correct. The same input, two assemblies: the over-broad set
proves the break, the empty set proves the fix. Injection lives in the assembly, not the store.

tasks.instruction:
In 4–6 sentences, for a non-technical colleague: explain where the "encrypted at rest" claim's
truth lives (the storage encryption SETTING plus its KEY reference — SC-28/CC6.1 — not any user
row) and where the "access is enforced" claim lives (the access policy/grant — AC-3 — not the
data), and why a returned row proves the DATA claim but never the at-rest or access claim. Use
the §3 three-filing-systems model and the §4.6 settings-not-rows point, not jargon.

hints.nudge: A row reads the same whether or not the disk is encrypted — so what would actually prove encryption-at-rest?

hints.concept: §4.6 — at-rest control-truth lives in settings + key references and access policy, not rows
